title: Mates make historic flight in hot air balloon over Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre
text:
A hot air balloon flight over Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre made history over the weekend, while narrowly avoiding wild weather.

After his trip to Europe was unexpectedly cancelled, Victorian Steve Timmis started brainstorming holiday ideas a little closer to home.

"I was in the pub with my son-in-law, Ben, and I said, 'I reckon I'm going to go up to Lake Eyre and have a look at that while its full … I reckon you should come up and we could fly a balloon across it'." Mr Timmis said.

" He'd already had a few beers, and he just agreed instantly … No good story starts with a salad, right? "

The team started doing some serious research, and took a reconnaissance trip to William Creek, where pilot Trevor Wright took them up for a flight to scope out the place.

On an early trip to William Creek, Trevor Wright took the crew up to check out the airspace. (Supplied: Steve Timmis)

Can't plan for the weather

At the start of August, Mr Timmis and a few members of the team began the trip back to William Creek where they would wait for the right conditions.

"The plan was we would allow two weeks, and the first week just nothing was happening, so we just hung around the Flinders Ranges and took our time to get up there until the weather started to look okay," Mr Timmis said.

Steve Timmis played the role of crew chief. (Supplied: Steve Timmis)

The remaining crew members journeyed from Mildura and Melbourne in time for a Saturday-morning take-off, just as a major weather event reached the state.

"We were mildly worried about the weather, but overnight the winds come up severely … Marree Airport was shut, they couldn't get off the ground," Mr Timmis said.

" We were having gusting, up to 30-knot winds, which was way too fast for us to set up a balloon. "

Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre at its fullest in years For the second year in a row, Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre is brimming with water.

With a post-flight drive to Marree and a downpour on the way, the team decided to pull the pin on the whole flight at 6am on Saturday.

"We sort of left the balloons half-packed up just in a slight slimmer of hope … [Then at] about 6:30 I spoke to Trevor [Wright]," Mr Timmis said.

"Trevor said 'Listen, at about sun-up, usually for half an hour or 45 minutes, there's always a bit of a lull out there.'

Ben Gowers piloted the Zircon balloon on his own. (Supplied: Steve Timmis)

"It was still too windy to set up, but we thought 'We'll roll out the balloons anyway so we're ready to go'. Because if there was a window it was only going to be for 10 or 15 minutes."

At about 7am, Mr Wright's intel pulled through.

"Things changed just ever so slightly and we were there ready," Mr Timmis said.

Balloons sat ready for a speedy take-off, just in case the weather came good. (Supplied: Steve Timmis)

"It was go, go, go, go, go. It was quite traumatic; you wouldn't have wanted it any faster. We were at the outer limits of what you could set up a balloon with the wind."

Hot air balloons are go

Ben Gowers piloted the rainbow balloon solo — just 18 months after gaining his licence — while Kiff and Paterson Saunders flew the second one.

The trip took them over expanses of water. (Supplied: Steve Timmis)

The flight took three hours and 40 minutes, covering 183 kilometres. The balloons reached speeds of about 80km per hour and soared to around 2,740 metres.

The flight spanned 183 kilometres. (Supplied: Steve Timmis)

"The wind down low was going the wrong way, but once they got up a little bit it was going the right way to go out above the main lake, and we got sort of three quarters of the way across that," Mr Timmis said.

"Then the guys dropped down and were able to come across Lake Eyre South as well, and right over the top of the Marree Man.

"It was really emotional. Traumatic, anxiety, very depressed early in the morning when we weren't going. But just so happy and so relieved that we got it done.

"It was truly a great experience."

Believed to be the first time a hot air balloon had been flown over the lake, there were no shortage of doubters in the lead up, Mr Timmis said.

Loading...

"The biggest question was, 'What happens if you land in the lake?' And realistically, there's no more danger of that really than an airplane running out of fuel and having to land in the lake," he said.

" The most dangerous part of the whole mission was being left in the pub unsupervised until the weather came good. "

When it rains…

After a successful flight, the balloons came down to land on the Oodnadatta Track, narrowly beating the rain.

"We had a quick beer there to celebrate, and then we jumped on the road to finish the last 80-odd kilometres into Marree," Mr Timmis said.

A post-landing beer on the Oodnadatta Track was much needed. (Supplied: Steve Timmis)

"We got into the pub, had our first beer there, and five minutes later the road was shut."

The morning after their grand adventure, Mr Timmis and his crew planned to put in a big day and drive the nearly 850km to Mildura.

But about 120kms in, just outside of Leigh Creek, they ran into road trouble.

"Everything from here south is closed, so we haven't finished yet … we can just hang around in Leigh Creek," Mr Timmis said.

It takes a village. (Supplied: Steve Timmis)

Mr Timmis and his team hope to see others do the same flight, or at the very least visit the blossoming outback.

"I would say anybody … if you're sitting at home in your lounge, get out and have a go," he said.

"Come and have a look at this country now, it is the best it has ever been. It's green and beautiful."

title: Commonwealth water policy blamed for loss of 78 jobs at rice giant
text:
Commonwealth water policy is being blamed for the loss of almost 80 jobs in the NSW Riverina region.

SunRice, one of the world's largest rice companies, employs about 650 people in the region, but foreshadowed in July that it would scale down its local operations due to low crop volumes brought on by drought and "water policy settings".

After a month of consultation with staff and unions, the company has now confirmed the loss of 78 jobs and changes to 92 positions across its Deniliquin and Leeton mills, as well as Australian Grain Storage.

SunRice Group CEO Paul Serra said in a statement that "we don't take these decisions lightly".

"Our focus has been on retaining as many employees as possible, including through redeployment opportunities where feasible," he said.

"SunRice continues to advocate to government on the adverse impacts of water policy settings on the Riverina rice industry."

Ricegrowers' Association of Australia president Peter Herrmann says it's a sad time for everyone involved. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

Peter Herrmann, the president of the Ricegrowers' Association of Australia, told ABC Riverina Breakfast it was a sad time for many people within the industry and the affected communities.

"We really feel it in the country when communities like ours are impacted by choices like this," he said.

The company will move from 24/7 production at Leeton to 16-hour shifts, five days a week.

Processing at its Deniliquin mill will still take place on five days per week, but hours will be cut from 24 to eight per day.

Federal government 'squarely responsible'

Leeton Shire Council general manager Jackie Kruger said 10 families in Leeton and 68 families in Deniliquin would be affected by the redundancies.

"We will work proactively with SunRice and the impacted staff to see if there's other businesses in Leeton that can absorb them," she said.

SunRice will move from 24/7 production at Leeton to 16-hour shifts, five days a week. (ABC Rural: Cara Jeffery)

Ms Kruger said the job cuts were a direct result of the federal government purchasing water from irrigators to meet targets in the Murray-Darling Basin Plan.

"Government water reform has impacted the rice industry … particularly from 2023, when the federal government brought in an amendment to the Restoring Our Rivers Act."

"These water buybacks have skewed the price of water and made water less available for annual croppers like rice farmers and cotton farmers.

" The government is squarely responsible for this decision that SunRice has had to make. "

The federal environment and water minister, Murray Watt, has been contacted for comment.

SunRice says it will continue to support employees whose roles have been impacted. (ABC Rural: Cara Jeffery)

A 2024 ABARES report foreshadowed that rice would be the crop most impacted by continued voluntary water purchases.

Production last summer was about 180,000 tonnes, the smallest crop since the 2019-20 drought.

During his maiden speech in federal parliament this week, One Nation's federal member for Farrer said the Murray-Darling Basin Plan was a failing, expensive ideological exercise.

"Environmental policy cannot be considered in isolation from food production, regional communities, national resilience and human wellbeing," David Farley said.

"Australia needs to have the courage to examine the Murray-Darling Basin Plan objectively."

title: Commonwealth Bank home loan applications fall 15pc since May
text:
Australia's largest home lender, the Commonwealth Bank, has seen home loan applications tumble 15 per cent since May, after three interest rate hikes and the federal budget's tax changes.

CBA's net profit rose 7 per cent over the last financial year, to $10.9 billion.

But the major bank has seen the early impact of the housing market downturn, as other big banks report similar hits to home loans, with Westpac reporting a 20 per cent decline in applications since May, while NAB flagged a 15 per cent fall.

"Housing activity has softened from a high base," CBA chief executive Matt Comyn said in a statement this morning.

"Application volumes appear to have stabilised in recent weeks."

Mortgages burdening households at record levels Who had it tougher on housing? These stats may put the generational debate to bed.

The bank said there has also been a 17 per cent decline in loan application volumes since last year.

Mr Comyn said mortgage activity appeared to be at its lowest in late June, with positive signs emerging from early August.

Asked how this would affect mortgage credit growth, Mr Comyn said the bank was now forecasting it to settle in a relatively narrow 4-5 per cent range over the year, albeit with some volatility.

But he noted while there were several factors contributing to a weakening housing sector, he also highlighted Australia's property market was coming off an unusually strong financial year, when credit growth and investor lending exceeded CBA's expectations.

Budget changes, rate hikes hit home loans

The major lenders have highlighted the decline in the mortgage market since May, as the federal budget was handed down on May 12.

It contained sweeping changes to Australia's property taxation rules, including only allowing real estate investors to negatively gear newly built properties.

But investors who owned existing properties before the budget would still be able to deduct their net rental losses against their wages and other personal income.

Three of the big four banks have reported a significant drop in home loan applications. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

The government also abolished the 50 per cent capital gains tax discount and replaced it with a discount based on inflation indexation, as existed prior to September 1999.

It has also introduced a 30 per cent minimum tax rate on net capital gains, with the changes meaning people selling investment properties could face more tax under the new regime.

The May timing of the downturn also reflects three interest rate hikes delivered by the Reserve Bank — in February, March and May, the latter coming the week before the federal budget.

CBA is now forecasting interest rates will remain on hold at 4.35 per cent for the rest of 2026, before "a couple of cuts" in 2027.

Mr Comyn said he expected some buyers to return to the market in anticipation of those lower rates.

Profit climbs but CBA sees economy slowing

The Commonwealth Bank's net profit rose 7 per cent over the year, to $10.87 billion. Cash earnings closed in on $11 billion.

CBA shareholders will receive a final dividend of $2.70 per share, fully franked, taking the total payout for the year to $5.05, 4 per cent higher than last year.

Its net interest margin (NIM) was a little lower, down 0.03 percentage points compared to the previous financial year, to 2.05 per cent.

The NIM captures the difference between the interest that the bank earns from lending money and the interest it pays on deposits.

ABC Business Daily The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news.

Operating expenses rose 6 per cent to $13.76 billion, which the bank said was driven by "inflation, investment in technology, fraud scams and financial crime, partly offset by productivity initiatives and favourable foreign exchange".

Offering his economic outlook, Mr Comyn said "growth is slowing, with higher interest rates and inflation placing uneven pressure on household incomes and economic activity", evidenced by households consuming fewer goods and services compared to five years ago.

CBA said it grew at or above the level of the broader banking system across it five major divisions: home lending, business lending, consumer finance, household deposits and business deposits.

"It is the first time CBA has achieved this and the first time any major Australian bank has done so in the past 15 years," the bank said.

CBA said it is "the main financial institution for one in three Australians and one in four Australian businesses".

title: Everything you need to know as Australia hosts Bangladesh in the Top End
text:
Australia is hosting Bangladesh in a rare Test series this August, as winter cricket hits the Top End.

The two teams will play two Tests, the first of which gets underway in Darwin on August 13 at Marrara Stadium.

The second starts on August 22 in Mackay, where Harrup Park will become the 12th ground to host a men's Test match in Australia.

You can listen to live coverage of both Tests on the ABC Listen App, or follow the ABC Sport live blog.

'Nowhere to hide' or free swing?: ABC Cricket Podcast

It is the first time in 23 years that Bangladesh will tour Australia for a Test series.

Here's everything you need to know.

When does Australia play Bangladesh?

The first Test gets underway on Thursday, August 13, with the first session starting at 10am ACST in Darwin, NT.

That means the start time is 10:30am AEST (Queensland, New South Wales, ACT, Victoria and Tasmania), 10:00am in South Australia and the Northern Territory, and 8:30am in Western Australia.

The second Test starts on Saturday, August 22, with the first ball again set to be bowled 10:00am AEST in Mackay, Queensland.

That is 10am in Queensland, New South Wales, ACT, Victoria and Tasmania, 10:30am in South Australia and the Northern Territory, and 8am in Western Australia.

Each Test is scheduled for five days.

Where are the Tests being played?

Australia played South Africa at Marrara Stadium last year in a T20 international. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

August is not normally cricket season in Australia, but officials are taking advantage of the dry season in the north to take these matches to the tropics, with Darwin and Mackay hosting the Test matches.

Darwin's Marrara Oval will host just its third ever men's Test match and first since Sri Lanka visited in July 2004.

Australia have a 100 per cent winning record in Tests in Darwin, winning by an innings and 132 runs against Bangladesh in 2003, following that up with a 149-run victory against Sri Lanka the year after.

Australia has also played four ODIs in Darwin, all against Bangladesh and all resulting in emphatic victories.

In T20Is it's a slightly different story though, with South Africa sharing the spoils across two matches at the venue last year.

Mackay's Harrup Park has never hosted a men's Test match before and will become the 12th venue in Australia to do so.

Harrup Park in Mackay will become the 12th ground to host a men's Test match in Australia. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

The ground did host a youth Test match last year between Australia and India's under 19 sides, a low-scoring match won by India by seven wickets.

There have been three ODIs at the ground, two of them involving Australia. Again, South Africa were the opponents in 2025 and, again, the spoils were shared.

The only other ODI took place during the 1992 Cricket World Cup between India and Sri Lanka.

Given that Mackay averages 313.2 millimetres of rain in February — the wettest month on average across the year for the city — it's perhaps not a surprise that rain meant that the match was abandoned after just two balls were bowled.

That was even after a helicopter hovered above the pitch in an attempt to dry it out.

Australia's women have played three ODIs (in 2021) and two T20Is (in 2024) at the ground, winning all but one game.

Who is playing?

Pat Cummins returns for Australia's first Test of the season. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Mark Brake)

Australia has named a strong squad, with front-line bowlers Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon all returning following their injury lay offs.

Such impressive bowling depth has seen Michael Neser miss out, the luckless Queenslander then suffering a hamstring injury in any case that will keep him out of contention.

It is, essentially, a full strength team, something Bangladesh skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto, is pretty impressed about.

"I personally liked the fact that they have chosen their full-strength team," he said earlier this month in an interview with ESPN Cricinfo.

"They are not taking us lightly. I think our team has earned this respect."

Najmul Hossain Shanto will lead Bangladesh in Australia. (Getty Images: Sameera Peiris)

Disappointingly for Bangladesh, they come into the series missing two key weapons in lightning-fast seamer Nahid Rana, who has been ruled out due to a left-side strain, and Shoriful Islam, who has a hurt hamstring.

Then, key spin bowler Taijul Islam suffered a blow to the hand in the warm up game and did not bowl at all in the second innings.

The 23-year-old Rana is one of the form bowlers in world cricket, capable of delivering the ball at speeds in excess of 150km/h. He has already taken 44 wickets in international cricket this year — the most by any bowler — at an average of 18.31.

On a positive note, Litton Das recovered from a calf injury he picked up during the home ODI series against Australia in June.

Batting is a problem for the tourists though — chief selector Habibul Bashar said the selection of 33-year-old lefty Soumya Sarkar was as a result of "a bit of desperation". Hardly a ringing endorsement for a man who has not played Test cricket since 2021.

Australia Squad Bangladesh Squad Pat Cummins (c) Najmul Hossain Shanto (c) Scott Boland Amite Hasan (wk) Alex Carey (wk) Ebadot Hossain Cameron Green Hasan Mahmud Josh Hazlewood Jaker Ali (wk) Travis Head Khaled Ahmed Josh Inglis (wk) Litton Das (wk) Marnus Labuschagne Mehidy Hasan Miraz Nathan Lyon Mominul Haque Steven Smith Musfik Hasan Mitchell Starc Mushfiqur Rahim (wk) Jake Weatherald Shadman Islam Beau Webster Soumya Sarkar Taijul Islam Tanzid Hasan Taskin Ahmed

Jake Weatherald, the first Northern Territorian to play a Test for Australia, was watching on in the crowd the last time the Australians played in Darwin.

He is a great chance to start on his home ground after a solid spell in the County Championship with Leicestershire, where he scored 483 runs at an average of 60.37, including scoring an unbeaten 104 against Glamorgan in Cardiff.

What form are Bangladesh in?

Bangladesh have only lost one of their last five Test matches. (Getty Images: Sameera Peiris)

Bangladesh come into this Test series off the back of a pretty decent run, having lost just one of their last five matches in the format.

Two thumping victories at home against Ireland in November 2025 were backed up by a hugely impressive 2-0 series victory against Pakistan in May this year.

That wasn't bad.

Now for the things that have been pretty poor.

A one off Test against Zimbabwe at the Harare Sports Club resulted in a calamitous defeat by an innings and 85 runs.

If that was bad, then the absolute thrashing the Cricket Australia XI delivered last week was even worse, the tourists bowled out for just 54 in their second dig as the CA XI won by an innings and 38 runs.

If it wasn't for Mehidy Hasan Miraz's unbeaten century in the first innings, rescuing his side from 6-110, who knows how bad the score would have looked as Corey Rocchiccioli took 6-83 in that first innings and Campbell Thompson took 8-25 in the second.

What is Bangladesh's record against Australia?

Jason Gillespie's stunning double century will go down in the annals as one of the best ever night watchman displays. (Getty Images: Hamish Blair)

Bangladesh have only ever played against Australia six times in their Test history — they've only played fewer Tests against Ireland (3) and Afghanistan (2) which, given Bangladesh have been a Test-playing nation since 2000, is a damning inditement on Australia's commitment to playing the minnows.

Somewhat surprisingly then, Bangladesh does have a Test victory against Australia to their name and, it was their most recent series in 2017.

Bangladesh claimed a stunning 20-run victory in Mirpur, with Shakib Al Hasan claiming player of the match honours after scoring a 133-ball 84 in the first innings and taking 5-85 with the ball in the final innings.

Australia got revenge in Chattogram, winning by seven wickets as Nathan Lyon took 7-94 and 6-60, while David Warner scored a brilliant, six-hour, 234-ball 123 in the first innings.

Australia's best ever batting performance in Chattogram though came 11 years before that, when night watchman Jason Gillespie scored a stunning unbeaten 201 to help Australia claim victory by an innings and 80 runs.

The first Test of that series in Fatullah had been won by the far more tense margin of three wickets, with Ricky Ponting's grinding 118 not out helping the Aussies over the line.

Bangladesh have never beaten Australia in Australia though, losing both their 2003 Tests by over an innings, in matches that took place in Darwin and Cairns.

title: What happens if you forgot to do the census last night?
text:
Have you completed the census yet?

Technically, census night was last night, but that doesn't mean you've missed the boat.

What happens if you don't do the census?

Don't worry, you can still complete the census.

"There is still time to complete your form after census night," an Australian Bureau of Statistics spokesperson said.

Get to it as soon as you can and you shouldn't have a problem.

When is the census due?

As soon as possible.

Census night was on August 11, but this doesn't mean people had to complete the census on that exact date.

It just means you have to answer questions about where you were on the night of August 11.

More than five million Australian households completed their forms early this year and the ABS expects quite a few households to submit their forms after census night.

A report about the 2021 census said the online census form was open for about 10 weeks.

And paper forms were accepted "for as long as practicable", with the last paper form included in the census received in December 2021.

That was months after the 2021 census night in early August.

Census night was on August 11, but you're able to complete your form after that date. (ABC News: Dannielle Maguire)

Do I have to do the census?

Yes, participating in the census is compulsory under the Census and Statistics Act 1905.

But you may not have to fill out a form yourself if someone in your household includes you and your information on the household form.

Almost everyone who is in Australia on census night must be included on a census form, including international students, visitors, visa holders and babies.

However, foreign diplomats and their families living in Australia are not included.

Is there a fine for not doing the census?

Yes, but that doesn't mean you'll be fined for being a few days late.

The ABS will contact you to encourage you to complete and submit your form first.

"We aim to get everyone to participate in the census voluntarily," an ABS spokesperson said.

If you don't respond to this gentle nudge, the ABS may serve you with a written direction to complete the census.

This is a formal legal instruction and if you fail to comply, you could be prosecuted and fined.

What is the fine for not doing the census?

If you're prosecuted for failing to comply with the legal instruction to complete the census, you could be fined up to $364 a day.

But remember, it doesn't have to come to that.

While we're on the topic of fines, it's also an offence to knowingly provide false or misleading statements or information in the census.

If you're prosecuted for this, you could face a fine of up to $3,640.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics aims to have people complete the census voluntarily. (ABC News: Dannielle Maguire)

What is the point of the census?

The data gathered from the census is really important.

It helps the government plan for the future.

Information collected via the census helps the government make decisions about things like health care, transport, schools and infrastructure.

How often is the census?

Every five years.

The last one was in 2021.

Worried about what happens to your answers?

The personal information you give on your census form is confidential and protected by law.

It is not shared with anyone else outside the ABS.

This means government agencies like the Department of Home Affairs, the Australian Taxation Office and Centrelink cannot see what you have written on your census form.

The data is handled by the Australian Bureau of Statistics, which is an independent statutory authority and an official organisation trusted by 90 per cent of the general community, according to an ABS survey last year.

"We have a range of processes and protections that make sure information on census forms stays confidential," an ABS spokesperson said.

"For example, we use the strongest encryption technology available to make sure information from the online census form is secure.

"People should be reassured that organisations [other government departments and marketing companies] can't access any personal information you include on your census form."

The legislation around the census also imposes strict secrecy obligations on all ABS employees.

What if I don't want my household to see my answers?

You are allowed to fill out your own form, separate to your household.

All you need to do is call the Census Contact Centre on 1800 181 227 and someone will either provide you with a census number to complete your Census online or send you your own paper form.

The ABS keeps the form with the most complete information about the person, so answer as many questions as you can in your separate form.

"To ensure your separate form is counted, we ask that you use the same name, date of birth and sex recorded at birth details as those recorded on the household form where possible," an ABS spokesperson said.

"You can then respond to other questions on the census form in the way that best reflects you."

Can I do the census online?

Yes.

You can either fill out a paper form or complete it on the ABS Census website.

The website should look like this:

The online census portal is available on the Australian Bureau of Statistics website. (Australian Bureau of Statistics)

You will need your census number to complete the form online.

Where do I find my census number?

Your home should have received an envelope from the ABS that looks like this:

Look for the Australian Bureau of Statistics logo and orange text. (ABC News: Dannielle Maguire)

Inside, there should be a letter containing a census number and a temporary password.

But if you don't have a census number, you can go to this website, where you'll be prompted to enter your mobile phone number so the ABS can text you a one-time PIN and your census number.

For help over the phone, you can call the Census Contact Centre on 1800 181 227.

title: 'Rude to say no': All Blacks icon performs solo haka against current team
text:
South African rugby teams love facing the haka. None have ever replied to New Zealand's traditional pre-match challenge with another haka until today.

Ma'a Nonu stepped in front of his new Sharks teammates and performed a solo haka in what will probably be the lasting memory of a tour match the New Zealanders won 54-0 at soggy Kings Park.

Nonu played 103 matches for New Zealand from 2003-15 and has continued playing around the world at age 44. The Sharks signed him a week ago to help develop their young players. Then as their injury list lengthened they drafted him onto the bench to face the All Blacks.

He was reluctant at first. He didn't want to detract from the Sharks' first match against the All Blacks in 30 years. He relented to help make up the numbers.

"I thought it would be rude to say no," Nonu told broadcaster SuperSport. "I thought I would put the boots on and try to help the team really."

For his first time facing the All Blacks, he talked to New Zealand assistant coaches Tana Umaga and Tamati Ellison on Monday about replying to the All Blacks' haka.

"Out of respect for our team and on behalf of myself and my family, I thought it was the right thing to do, to answer the boys and the All Blacks," Nonu said.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

So after lining up for the anthems, then watching the haka, he stood alone with the Sharks arrayed behind him, and the All Blacks lined up on the other side of halfway. He performed the All Blacks' own haka, Kapa o Pango, to initial silence from the crowd and growing cheers.

Afterward, he nodded to the All Blacks, many of whom nodded back. Only Codie Taylor and Beauden Barrett still play for New Zealand from Nonu's last squad.

"It was such a privilege and an honour, and to do the haka, showing my respect on behalf of my family to the team I love," Nonu said.

He got into the game with a quarter to go. His first touch was to clatter into flyhalf Ruben Love, who was 2 years old when Nonu debuted for New Zealand.

"I got 20 minutes. I tried my best. It was great to see the [New Zealand] boys," he said.

"The All Blacks opened up in the last 30 minutes and I was chasing my tail. Credit to them, they're improving, and all the best to the brothers for the next game."

AP

title: History beckons for Phil Sami after the hard life of a Gold Coast hero
text:
As the weather gets warmer and the dreams of the NRL's elite become all the more real, the competition strugglers begin the march towards the end.

If South Sydney defeats Canterbury on Friday night the ninth-placed Bulldogs will be two wins outside the top eight with just three rounds remaining and their play-off hopes will feel more mathematical than truly possible.

It means, with the top eight all bust set in stone, the nine clubs who will miss out on the finals in 2026 face four matches with uncertain stakes.

Careers will begin for the young as some look to the future and end for the old as others celebrate the past on their way out the door.

Tedious debates about a potential wildcard round or expanded finals series, where games are called "content" as they transform into mere vessels for revenue, will be reheated.

Spoiling the dreams of their betters becomes the greatest prize a struggling team can hope for and incessant mentions of how one side or another is only "playing for pride" will instead merely compound their shame.

Sami has been one of Gold Coast's best during some of the club's hardest times. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

It is amidst this wreckage that Phillip Sami, who has lived the hard life of a Gold Coast legend, will try and make history.

Sami is currently level with Anthony Don as the Titans all-time leading try-scorer with 85 and he has four games to land one more and leave for St George Illawarra at season's end as the top dog.

It would be a just reward for a decade spent fighting for a cause that seems to be perpetually starting over.

Counting interims, Sami has played under nine head coaches in his 10 seasons with Gold Coast.

He's played in just one semi-final, which doubles as the Titans only finals match since 2010, and has never played on a team with a winning record.

Sami debuted for Gold Coast back in 2017. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

He has been through it, as anybody who sticks around long enough to hold a Gold Coast record must, which means he knows these curious final weeks of the season very well.

Expect more of his best because if the lure of premierships was all that drove Sami he would have shot through long ago and he wouldn't be here now, on the verge of claiming the record.

A cynic might say it's a modest piece of history. Of all the clubs that have existed for as long as the Titans have or more, only Western Suburbs Magpies have a lower total for their top try-scorer.

But only a snob turns up their nose when a house record is concerned and given Gold Coast always have to fight to make themselves heard, Sami has done more for that fight than most.

He's chased this record the hard way. Given the club's point-scoring struggles and playmaker upheaval over the years, sparkling backline efforts have rarely been easy to find and there are precious few catch and fall efforts to be found here.

But every now and then, Sami goes big-game hunting and when he does he seems to have a special talent for winning battles using the weapons of his enemies.

One of the first times he showed this quality was in 2018 against the Warriors when Samis scored what remains his greatest try.

In those days, getting a hand on the light-stepping Roger Tuivasa-Sheck was like catching smoke and Sami, in just his second year of first grade, didn't so much give that year's Dally M medallist a taste of his own medicine but a lethal overdose.

Sami did the same when he flew over Clint Gutherson during the days when Parramatta really was the latter's kingdom before hitting him with his own celebration dance.

He showed he's not lost his touch earlier this season when he rounded Reece Walsh en route to a 70-metre solo effort that left the prince of Brisbane grasping at ghosts as Sami howled like a wolf.

It's not just with tries or even with football — Sami has a rare gift for being larger than life.

When he played two matches for Queensland back in 2020 a coach from his schoolboy days detailed the time Sami outran a kangaroo during a match.

It sounds like something from a folk song but rap is more Sami's speed given Goodna rapper Lisi shouted him out on a track later that same year.

At the time he was best known for the step on Tuivasa-Sheck and the moment he ran down ran down Josh Addo-Carr, which came at a time when that was like shooting Jesse James.

That try-saver, like his all-round play this year, is proof there's more to his game than just the fun stuff.

Sami has run more metres than any other player in the league, over 200 more than second place and 500 more than the next best winger. He's averaging 218 metres gained per game, the best mark of his career by miles.

He's also top when it comes to post-contact metres, a full 400 metres ahead of any other flanker, and teammate Keano Kini is the only player in the whole NRL who's run the ball more times.

Throw in that Sami only needs one more line break and one more try will match his career-best total for a single season in both categories and you can make a hipster's case he's a shot for one of the wing spots in the Dally M team of the year, making his progress towards the record an even more furious charge.

He has given his absolute best in service of one last fresh start for the Titans and perhaps this will even be the one that sticks.

Gold Coast fans have plenty to be optimistic about in the years to come. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

In Kini, Jayden Campebll, Zane Harrison and Oliver Pascoe, Gold Coast have a spine of playmakers that feels full of exciting possibilities.

Josh Hannay has shown some promising signs as coach, displaying a sharp eye for the kind of fighters the Titans will need in the years to come.

One more win will give them more victories than last year and they're a chance of finishing above Brisbane for just the sixth time in their history.

In a broader sense, after two decades the club has found a lived-in quality by sitting more comfortably with it's own history as an enticing future beckons.

Why Gold Coast has already won Magic Round One of the best parts of Magic Round is going jersey-spotting but before a ball is kicked in Brisbane the Titans have already cleaned up via their Chargers-inspired retro strip.

Sami will not be on hand to see it. He's taken up a three-year deal with St George Illawarra, one which was too good to refuse even as the Titans were open to keeping him.

So he has four games left to get one last try. The first chance is against Newcastle on Sunday and it won't be easy.

The Knights have defied their bulging casualty ward in recent weeks to keep themselves in the race for the top four and will be warm favourites at home.

But Sami has never had it easy and no Titan ever really does, so why should the moment of achievement for club and player be any different?

They've lived through dark days together, enough for both know it's how to take the shiny moments where you find them, regardless of how and when they come.

When you are in the final days of a lost year a player can either accept that fate or try and change it on the hope that this game can be better than the last just because it's a fresh start.

Sami has spent his career believing that and proving it with his actions. He wouldn't have scored these tries and lasted this long if he didn't.

Now he has a chance at a prize all his own, that he has fought for his own way and if he can break the record before leaving it will mark his ultimate reward — to live as a Gold Coast hero.

That title tells the tale of a hard footballing life but someone had to live it and Sami has lived it all the way.

title: The Office star Lucy Davis announces she has incurable cancer
text:
Actress Lucy Davis, best known for her role as Dawn Tinsley on the UK version of The Office, has announced she has "incurable" stage 4 breast cancer.

In a post on Instagram, Davis revealed she had been diagnosed one-and-a-half years ago and the cancer had metastasised to her bones including her spine, right hip and ribs.

"The cancer is incurable, and too late for chemo," Davis said.

"The initial lump that I felt, wasn't a 'lump' as such; rather a kind of hard spot. Really tiny. I almost didn't bother getting it checked.

"So I guess I'm saying don't ignore anything — get everything checked out."

According to the National Breast Cancer Foundation, breast cancer is the second most commonly diagnosed cancer in Australia, after prostate cancer, with more than 20,000 people in Australia diagnosed every year.

Lucy Davis read out the Ring the Bell poem in her Instagram post. (Instagram: reallucydavis)

Stage 4 breast cancer, sometimes known as metastatic or advanced breast cancer, is when the disease has spread to other parts of the body. There is currently no cure; however, treatment is available to manage the illness and extend life.

Davis, who has also starred in Shaun of the Dead, Wonder Woman and The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina, said she was now trying bring as much fun into the rest of her life as possible.

"I always like to find the teachable moments in anything negative that happens. And cancer has not disappointed in that regard; there's a lot I have learned from it, and I'm grateful for that," she said.

In the post, Davis reads out the poem Ring the Bell, which is traditionally read after a patient completes chemotherapy or radiation treatment and rings a bell just once instead of the usual three times.

She described the pain she is in and said she would sometimes need to use a wheelchair.

"The thing that has been most vital to me is humour," Davis said.

"I asked my friends and family to make fun of me as much as possible (which they're really good at), and most importantly of all to not treat me like a sick person.

" There's nothing that will make you feel more unwell than being treated as if you're unwell. "

She said she was not scared of what was next and she planned to continue her work for animal rights.

Davis is a long-term vegan and a vocal animal activist. In 2007, she posed nude for PETA's campaign against the Guards Division's continued use of traditional bearskin caps.

The Office co-star Ricky Gervais left a heart comment on Davis's post.

"For those of you on a similar journey to mine, I do wish you well," she wrote.

"Cancer asks a lot from us, physically and mentally. And we all get to do it however we choose."

title: Live: ASX drops, CBA beats expectations with $10.9b profit
text:
CBA's investor presentation often yields some interesting information about the broader economy, given it is by far the nation's biggest bank.

One graph in particular offers an insight into both why property prices are falling and how that might help first home buyers.

The borrowing capacity of investors buying established properties has fallen. (CBA)

This graph shows how borrowing capacity across the board has fallen as interest rates rose three times between February and May.

That's because the banks have to test serviceability against these higher rates, reducing how much they can lend to a borrower on any given income level.

That's going to push property prices down, because people have a smaller maximum bid than they did six months earlier.

But the dotted orange line shows how the negative gearing change has the effect that the Albanese government is seeking, which is to level the playing field between investors and owner-occupiers.

Before the removal of negative gearing on purchases of established (already lived-in) properties, investors could borrow more than owner-occupiers because they could write-off some of the interest costs against their income tax bill.

But after the change, the maximum borrowing capacity of investors is much closer to owner-occupiers.

So a prospective investor and first home buyer on the same income, rocking up to the same auction, now have roughly similar maximum limits on how much they can bid.

This other chart from CBA is also telling. It shows what income level most home buyers have.

Around three-quarters of peroperty investors earn more than $200,000 a year. (CBA)

Around 50% of owner-occupier buyers and about three-quarters of investors have household incomes above $200,000 a year.

Given the surge in property prices in most housing markets across Australia, it's not really surprising that it's mostly high-income households who are applying for loans and buying home.

But it's not a great omen for the Great Australian Dream, where anyone with a stable full-time job should be able to aspire to own their own home.

title: Homeless mother's baby taken away while waiting for social housing
text:
Hannah* says she wept for several days after Child Safety officers turned up at Redcliffe Hospital to take her two-day-old baby away.

Hannah's name has been changed by the ABC for legal reasons.

"It hurts a lot," Hannah said.

"At times during the day I'm sitting there reminiscing on the memory of giving birth and how beautiful she was when I held her."

Hannah has spent the last two-and-a-half years living in a tent at a homeless encampment.

Shortly after her baby's birth officers gave Hannah a Temporary Assessment Order, which allows officers to seize a baby while they prepare a full report.

Hannah with her newly born baby. (Supplied)

She said she has not yet been given written reasons for her baby's seizure but believes it is due, at least in part, to her homeless living conditions.

The tent city she lives in does not have access to running water, electricity, bins, or toilets.

Hannah said she has applied for social housing and emergency housing, but has not yet received any offers.

In its 2026 budget the Queensland Government cut $42 million from the emergency housing program.

The latest department figures show there are 56,680 Queenslanders on the social housing waiting list.

Relying on the kindness of strangers

Ian Baskin has been cooking food for homeless people. (612 ABC: Kenji Sato)

While Hannah waits for social or emergency housing, she has been relying on charities to survive.

Ian Baskin runs the charity Neighbours4Neighbours and has been cooking food for homeless people.

Mr Baskin said it was an indictment on Australian society that mothers like Hannah were living in tents because of a housing crisis.

"Our building industry is stretched, stretched, stretched because it's not too many years until we've got the Olympics happening here," Mr Baskin said.

" This is all great — but what about people? Do people really matter? "

The Department of Housing and the Department of Child Safety said they could not comment on Hannah's case because of privacy laws.

A Department of Housing spokesperson said the state government was committed to delivering social housing.

"The Queensland Government is committed to helping Queenslanders in housing need," the spokesperson said.

"The Queensland Government has also committed to a $450 million boost to Specialist Homelessness Services (SHS) and crisis support in this year's state budget that will ensure more than $1 billion is delivered for homelessness services over the next four years."

The Temporary Assessment Order forbids Hannah from seeing her baby without an authorised officer in the room.

Hannah said visiting her baby in the department office had filled her with grief.

"She is my baby," Hannah said.

"She's been ripped from my arms, ripped from my heart, ripped from every part of me."

title: After 80 years of dairying, no-one wants this farm's milk
text:
A devastated Queensland dairy farmer fears he will be forced to cull his prized herd of 600 Brown Swiss cows if he can't find a processor to buy his milk.

Earlier this year Jason Rozynski's family celebrated 80 years of dairying on their home farm but now fear it could be their last.

Jason Rozynski has worked to build up his Brown Swiss dairy herd. (Supplied: Payton Rozynski)

Independent processor Maleny Dairies informed Mr Rozynski in June his contract to supply milk would not be renewed.

"On Friday, we'll be four weeks from not having anywhere to send our milk," Mr Rozynski said.

" We … are absolutely shocked to think that we could be in a situation where we have to meatworks (slaughter) those cows and close down. "

Maleny Dairies co-owner Ross Hopper said it was a "business decision" to end the decade-long supply relationship.

"It's not our intention to be mongrels," Mr Hopper said.

"It's just business, and we don't want to go down in a heap; otherwise, there'd be more farmers disrupted."

The Rozynskis began developing their Brown Swiss herd 20 years ago. (Supplied: Payton Rozynski)

It comes just six months after farmers, processors and the state government launched the 2026-2032 Queensland Dairy Plan, which aimed to lift the volume of milk produced in the state by five per cent.

As cheaper southern milk pours over the border, industry representatives say without stable processing capacity, any effort to increase production will turn sour.

Nowhere to go

The Rozynski family produces about 3.3 million litres of milk from two farms near Imbil in the Mary Valley, about 170 kilometres north of Brisbane.

Lisa Rozynski is proud of her daughter Payton, who plans to study veterinary science. (ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols)

As his 17-year-old daughter Payton competed in the dairy judging competition at the Ekka, Mr Rozynski contemplated the farm's future.

"We're so involved in the dairy industry and I've always been positive and proactive with it," Mr Rozynski said.

" You just wonder how on earth we could end up in this situation. "

Farmers return to Qld dairy industry After decades of dramatic decline, the number of dairy farms in Queensland has stabilised, and the industry is starting to rebuild.

He said the family was "extremely hurt" by Maleny Dairies' decision, but at first they were confident they could find a new processor.

"Normally that wouldn't be a problem," Mr Rozynski said.

"You'd ring around some other processors and get pricings and pick which one best suited to your farm.

" We did that … and everybody said their books are closed and there's no room. "

Angus, 15, (pictured with Lisa, Payton and Jason) hopes to be the fourth generation of the Rozynski family in the dairy industry. (ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols)

The Rozynski's were featured at the launch of the new Dairy Plan in February, which processors Norco, Bega Cheese, Lactalis Australia, and Dairy Farmers all signed up to.

None have agreed to buy the Rozynski's milk.

"It's just mind blowing to think that we do a really good job with our milk, high quality, great animal welfare … and we can't find a home for our milk," he said.

Ross Hopper in front of a new robot in the cold room at Maleny Dairies, November 2019. (ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols)

Maleny Dairies purchases milk from 11 farms in south-east Queensland, employs more than 50 workers at their processing plant, and has invested millions of dollars in efficiencies, including robotics.

Mr Hopper said currently there was an oversupply of milk in the state.

"This year we've got too much milk," he said.

"We've had to reduce our oversupply — it's just economics."

A robot at work in the cold room at Maleny Dairies, November 2019. (ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols)

About half of the milk Queenslanders consume, an estimated 250-300 million litres a year, comes from interstate.

Mr Hopper said Maleny Dairies, like other processors, had purchased milk from interstate — but only when local supply was low.

"When things aren't lining up … we've got to adjust our contracts to suit and adjust our milk flow and volumes," he said.

" We didn't think that finding another processor (for the Rozynskis) would be that hard. "

He said in the past the company sent excess milk to another processor at a loss, but that arrangement had ended.

Over and under supply

Dairy farmer Tim Bale advocates for the industry in NSW and Qld as the president of EastAUSmilk.

NSW dairy farmer Tim Bale was elected president of EastAusMilk in 2026. (ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols)

He said several factors, including the sale of Lactalis's historic South Brisbane factory in July for redevelopment, were affecting processing capacity.

"Some of Norco's milk was going through there," Mr Bale said.

" Now Norco has a greater volume of milk they've got to deal with, and they've got issues there just dealing with their excess. "

Historic South Brisbane milk factory to close Queensland's largest and oldest milk processing plant will close in South Brisbane in July, opening development opportunities for the valuable riverfront site.

Mr Bale said Woolworths' decision to phase out its Farmers Own brand, which buys direct from three farms in Qld and five in NSW, had "added to the chaos" as those farmers also sought to find a new home for their milk.

A spokesperson from Woolworths said it was consulting those farmers about the upcoming contract expiry.

"We are working closely with our suppliers and will continue to honour our contract terms, which includes an option for farmers to extend the contract for an extra 12 months," she said.

Norco and Lactalis were also contacted for comment.

title: Drastic measures older buyers are taking to save for their own home
text:
Luxury new builds and multi-million-dollar homes have made the streets where John Atwood grew up almost unrecognisable to him.

In the nearly four decades since he first moved away from the Gold Coast, the city has undergone an undeniable transformation.

Buying back into the city's property market has meant the 53-year-old has had to make some sacrifices.

Chief among them: moving back in with his elderly mother.

"I think we anticipated maybe spending a couple of months at my mum's place and saving up for a deposit," he said.

"It's been three and a half years now.

" Having grown up in the street we're now living in, we've seen [house prices] go from bugger all to astronomical prices in our area. "

Sacrifices to save a deposit

Property prices have skyrocketed since the COVID-19 pandemic, with the median home now selling for about $1 million.

The rental market can be even harder to crack, with the Gold Coast overtaking Sydney as the country's most expensive place to rent.

Gold Coast property price boom Gold Coast property prices have outpaced every Australian capital city over the past five years.

In an effort to beat that, Mr Atwood and his wife rent a portion of his mum's five-bedroom property for a fraction of what they'd pay elsewhere.

"If we'd gone on the standard rental market, I doubt we would have anything left over," he said.

Mr Atwood says moving back in with his mother has been a means to an end that will enable him and his wife to buy a house next year.

"The only thing is having to live with your mum after all these years, which is at times challenging."

The sacrifice has started to pay off, with the couple now feeling as though they've scraped together enough of a deposit to put home ownership in reach.

Gold Coast Australia's most expensive rental market Real estate experts say the Gold Coast's high concentration of luxury housing and persistent shortages in new construction are sustaining upward pressure on rentals.

"I think we may be able to do it next year, but age 53 … it does concern me going into retirement," Mr Atwood said.

"That [home] would probably not be paid off, and that's after even owning a place [in a previous marriage]."

Growing number of retirees have mortgage debt

By 2031, peak housing body National Shelter estimates 440,000 older households will be unable to find or afford suitable housing.

CEO Jackson Hills said that was sending more people towards retirement with major debt.

Jackson Hills says housing affordability has worsened significantly across the country. (ABC Radio Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

"This is an issue and we're seeing it for people going through separations or other life circumstances … people don't have the safety net to be able to meet a deposit hurdle," Mr Hills said.

With more people moving to the Gold Coast each week, he said it was critical to have a range of housing options available in the city to cater to different income groups.

"We've seen an escalation of people on lower incomes being forced to relocate from urban areas out to the fringes," Mr Hills said.

"When that's forced upon you, it's an entirely different thing … we need a variety of housing options."

The median house price on the Gold Coast has tipped $1-million. (ABC News: Glenn Mullane)

Home ownership rates slip

Mr Atwood's tale of moving back home to save a deposit is far from a one-off, according to Bond University property expert Dr Johari Amar.

Dr Amar said she was aware of four adults in her circle that were in a similar situation.

"Home ownership is decreasing on the Gold Coast and Queensland," she said.

"ABS data in 1996 sat at 80 per cent. By 2021 that dropped to 72 per cent."

Dr Amar says people moving back in with parents has become commonplace. (ABC News: Glenn Mullane)

With an influx of internal migration to the city, estimated to be more than 400 new residents to the Gold Coast each week, Dr Amar said more people were competing for the same number of homes, forcing prices up further.

"If there's no new supply … people who have got extra income would be able to outbid other people that cannot afford so that's where the issue sits," she said.

The solution isn't straightforward, with concerns Queensland embracing the abolishment of stamp duty for buyers out of the market for five years, like in the ACT, could worsen the already booming market.

"It could work but, without new supply, we're still competing for the same number of homes, so again it's making sure there's a balance between supply and demand," Dr Amar said.

Mr Atwood and his wife feel positive that by next year they'll be able to buy. (ABC News: Glenn Mullane)

For now, the first sign of a market cooling is giving Mr Atwood hope.

"For us, that's a good sign, the house prices are sort of coming down a bit … we'll hopefully be able to buy next year," he said.

title: Trump says FIFA would be making 'terrible mistake' to remove Infantino
text:
Embattled FIFA leader Gianni Infantino has a powerful and vocal supporter — US President Donald Trump.

As football organisations around the world continue to call for the resignation of the FIFA president, post-World Cup, Trump blasted that idea in a message he posted to Truth Social on Monday night.

"FIFA would be making a terrible mistake if, for any reason, they even considered replacing President Gianni Infantino," Trump wrote.

How Gianni Infantino's FIFA leadership imploded over two weeks The FIFA president has faced more than a fortnight of international turmoil, embroiled in a World Cup sell-off saga that sparked loss of confidence in his leadership.

"He is fantastic, having just presided over the most successful World Cup, by four times, ever presented. If he is gone, it will never be as successful or profitable again!"

UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North America, Central America and the Caribbean) and the AFC (Asia) banded together earlier in the week to release an open letter, signed by the president and general secretary of each organisation, urging Infantino's resignation.

Infantino has been under fire since last month's failed plan to launch the FIFA Forward Enterprise, which would have sold part of the World Cup's commercial rights to private investors to raise billions of dollars.

He apparently caused further damage by holding a crisis meeting last week in Morocco with some members of FIFA's management team.

Trump is a close ally of Infantino's after the FIFA boss awarded him the FIFA Peace Prize. (Getty Images: Kevin Dietsch)

"This recent meeting, where a select number of members of the FIFA Management Committee — not the full Committee — were summoned abroad, rather than leadership going to Zurich to address the heart of FIFA, its staff, only reinforces these concerns and represents a continuation of the very pattern of conduct that brought us to this moment," reads the letter from UEFA, CONCACAF and AFC.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"It is not the conduct of a custodian of the game, but of one who believes the game is answerable to him. There is silence where there should be accountability, distance where there should be openness.

"These are not the qualities football deserves in its leadership. That is why we have taken this stance: not lightly and not alone, but together, and out of duty to the game we serve."

Also Monday, US Soccer and others issued their own statement backing CONCACAF.

"US Soccer, Canada Soccer, CFU (Caribbean Football Union) and UNCAF (Central American Football Union) stand together, along with our colleagues around the world, in calling for meaningful change that strengthens FIFA's governance, transparency and accountability," the statement read.

Infantino, 56, has served as FIFA president since his initial election on February 26, 2016. His current term runs through 2027, and he has announced his bid for re-election to extend his tenure to 2031.

title: 'Scary' task removed with free period products in all ACT public schools
text:
All ACT public school students will now be able to access free period products without having to ask, following lobbying from Canberra students.

The initiative, which aims to end period poverty, provides free sanitary products via dispensers in bathrooms at all public primary schools, high schools, and colleges.

The program started as a pitch from a group of Canberra High School students at an International Women's Day conference in 2021.

A pilot of the program ran at the school for a year, and formed part of a report to the education minister about the value of making menstrual products readily available and accessible to students.

Last year, the ACT government said they were now accessible in more than 30 schools, and that has since been expanded to include 90 of 93 public schools.

The full rollout to the remaining schools will take place over the coming weeks.

But a key element of the program is that they are easily accessible.

Year 9 student Emily Duffy (left) says the dispersers have been a safety net for her to know she can access menstrual products without asking if she runs out. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

Removing the 'awkward' task of asking

The ACT became the first jurisdiction in Australia to guarantee access to free period products in 2023, but the program includes the caveat that those free pads and tampons should be available without having to ask.

Year 9 Canberra High School student Emily Duffy said having dispensers in bathrooms that can be accessed at any time has been "a really good safety net".

"They've always been there for me in my time at high school, but [before] you'd have to go to the front office, or you could ask a friend," Ms Duffy said.

"And obviously for some people it's very awkward and scary, a bit daunting maybe.

"[So] it's really good to just have those and not need to ask anyone."

Year 8 student Flick Hearne (right) says she has not heard any students express negative opinions about the period product dispensers. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

Year 8 student Flick Hearne agreed the dispensers "definitely made it a lot less awkward" for students to access free menstrual products when they need them.

"My friends have all said good things about it," Ms Hearne said.

" I haven't actually heard a negative thing about it at all. "

Canberra High School's executive teacher of science, Laura Gibbs, mentored the students when they pitched the idea in 2021 and engaged with the ACT Education Directorate, Minister for Education and fellow students and teachers to launch the pilot.

She said the dispensers were being regularly refilled, with some students taking multiple products for use outside school as well as while in class.

"A lot of them are also taking them home because they don't have access at home — or they're taking them home for parents, for friends, for other family members," Ms Gibbs said.

Canberra High School teacher Laura Gibbs says the program has seen a significant reduction in the rate of students missing days of school due to being on their period. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

"I knew that period poverty was a thing, but it wasn't until these students made me aware of it, that [I realised] it was such a big thing here at our school.

"I thought we were somewhat sheltered from that, but we went from 33 per cent of students having missed at least one day of school because of period poverty down to three per cent after we installed the products.

" For me, that just speaks for itself. Why would this not be available everywhere? "

Ms Gibbs said despite period products being available for free in ACT public schools since 2023, the way students had to ask for them could be "humiliating".

"So if you go to the bathroom, you realise before it's too late that you've got your period and you need something, you have to then MacGyver some kind of solution and then make your way to the front office and ask someone for a pad or a tampon," she said.

"That is such a dehumanising experience that so many students have been through, so we really wanted to push for them being accessible."

Laura Gibbs says the program is a great start, but more needs to be done to improve period education for students who do not menstruate. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

Ms Gibbs added that while the program's jurisdiction-wide expansion was "fantastic news", period education in ACT public schools remained "inadequate".

"There needs to be more education for all students of all sexes about what periods are, to make them normal," she said.

"There's a lot of gender division in how the education's done, I think we've got a lot of ways to go in that space.

"But I think this is a great step forward to making that conversation more comfortable to then be able to have a lot more education around it."

title: Emergency rescue deal secured for nation’s biggest aluminium smelter
text:
Australia’s biggest aluminium smelter is set to receive a major bailout package following long-running crisis negotiations with the federal and NSW governments over ways to keep the plant open and safeguard more than 1000 jobs.

Tomago Aluminium, majority-owned by resources giant Rio Tinto, started consulting the smelter’s workforce and their union officials late last year about the risk of the site having to close when its existing power contract expires in 2028 and its cost of electricity is set to double.

Tomago’s owners and government officials have been in crisis talks over assistance to keep the smelter viable beyond 2028.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and NSW Premier Chris Minns are expected to attend the smelter near Newcastle to announce the multi-year deal on Thursday, according to industry sources not yet authorised to speak publicly about the agreement.

The deal – at an unknown cost – would mark in the latest in a series of taxpayer-funded rescue packages to prop up struggling metals processors over the past two years after the Albanese government contributed to bailouts of Glencore’s Queensland copper smelter and refinery, Nyrstar’s smelters in Port Pirie and Hobart, and the collapsed Whyalla steelworks.

There is fascination across the competition about whether the clubs that miss out on Butters will bank the money budgeted for him and front-end contracts of existing players, or pivot to another big-name option. It is a similar story with Adelaide, who are trying to lure premiership star Zac Bailey out of Brisbane. Collingwood also have dual Brownlow medallist and free agent Lachie Neale in their sights, two years after they used that player movement mechanism to recruit ex-Giant Harry Perryman. Veteran GWS forwards Jesse Hogan and Jake Stringer, as well as out-of-favour Hawk Calsher Dear (who has a two-year offer from Hawthorn on the table), are on the Magpies’ radar, too, but it is unclear if they would be looking to recruit only one or more of them. This masthead has spoken to a range of sources – from clubland to player agents – who were granted anonymity to openly discuss the player-movement market.

A Humphrey trade is unlikely Contracted Sun Bailey Humphrey seems almost certain to remain at the Gold Coast next year despite multiple suitors – including Melbourne, Carlton and Hawthorn – tracking his progress throughout the season. Humphrey, who is contracted until the end of 2028, caused a stir when a photo surfaced of him meeting with new Demons coach Steven King and assistant Nathan Jones in October last year. Melbourne are in the process of trying to re-sign unrestricted free agent Tom Sparrow and are keen on agile Hawthorn’s Dear, but would prioritise talented forward-midfielder Humphrey if circumstances changed on his availability. The Suns refused to consider trading him last year, and Humphrey has not made a trade request this year. The Hawks are readying to bring in Gold Coast’s restricted free agent spearhead Ben King – with the Suns highly likely to accept a compensation pick rather than force a trade – and still want to trade for former Essendon captain Zach Merrett. The Blues acquired Ben Ainsworth from Gold Coast last year, plus ex-Swans Will Hayward and Ollie Florent, but are likely to remain aggressive with Chris Davies and Graham Wright overseeing list management. Decision time looms Carlton’s must-win clash against the Western Bulldogs on Sunday will be something of an audition for Bulldogs defender Buku Khamis as he weighs up his future at the club.

The Bulldogs upped their offer to the free agent to four years to match, in tenure, the offer from Carlton as they attempt to retain the popular Khamis. Versatile Bulldogs defender Buku Khamis. Getty Images The 26-year-old will spend the next fortnight, at least, deciding his future after examining offers from both clubs, with the Bulldogs increasingly hopeful he will remain at “the Kennel”. Khamis wanted to join the Blues at the end of last season as he felt starved of opportunity, but this season has proven the key role he can play at the Dogs. He has played every match, but is aware he is best suited as a third tall defender who intercepts in the air rather, than as a key defender expected to lock down opponents.

Cody Walker watch The one downside to Carlton’s on-field resurgence under interim coach Josh Fraser is that the equation to match a draft bid on prized father-son midfielder Cody Walker becomes that much harder. A south-east Queensland council appears to have taken a dig at its own mayor in a submission to a parliamentary inquiry, recommending any councillor on extended leave should be subject to a misconduct investigation. Redland City Council mayor Jos Mitchell has been on medical leave since May. The council recently said she would not return until at least the end of October, with deputy mayor Julie Talty in her chair. Jos Mitchell has been on leave since May. Dan Peled The council of Redlands, south-east of Brisbane, has been a hotbed of discontent for years, leading the state in conduct complaints received by the Office of the Independent Assessor in the 2024-25 financial year and the first half of 2025-26.

Advertisement

Of the 1008 complaints received in 2024-25, 114 were about Redlands councillors. Mitchell was the subject of about 50 in the 18 months after she elected as mayor, and she alleged they were used as a political tool against her. The former Labor state government reformed the OIA to streamline its processes in 2023, and the current LNP government made further changes to narrow its scope in March this year, before announcing a parliamentary inquiry into the councillor conduct framework in June. Redlands led the state in OIA complaints last year. Matt Dennien The inquiry, run by the Local Government, Small Business and Customer Service Committee, is considering the effectiveness of the current system – based around the OIA and the Councillor Conduct Tribunal – and potential changes to the Local Government Act. It received 40 submissions before they closed this week, with the Redlands submission including a pointed recommendation apparently directed at its own mayor.

Advertisement

“The definition of ‘misconduct’, which will continue to be a discipline matter, needs to be broadened to include the more serious councillor conduct breaches and to address non-performance, not just bad behaviour,” it said. “As we have seen, a councillor can effectively avoid accountability by simply being absent. A councillor on extended leave should then be subject to a misconduct investigation.” Related Article Queensland councils ‘Loopholes’ in council complaints system can be weaponised: mayor Mitchell’s leave has been the subject of heated online debate since May, with other councillors and former local federal MP and mayoral candidate Andrew Laming often weighing in. The mayor has been largely silent, but posted on Facebook this month claiming there was “a fair bit of fake news” about her absence.

Advertisement

“I’ve been dealing with a number of health issues, one requiring major surgery and recuperation, over the last 12 weeks,” she wrote. “I have of course provided medical certificates and I am focused on recovery … I look forward to returning as soon as possible.” That post followed a now-deleted Facebook post, written by her family members, taking aim at local government department boss Bronwyn Blagoev for what they deemed politically opportunistic comments following the departure of a department-appointed governance adviser at the council. “The mayor’s prolonged absence meant that key opportunities to address critical governance challenges and foster stronger leadership were missed,” Blagoev had said. The Redlands submission also called for a properly resourced external body to investigate councillor conduct outside the OIA, stronger penalties, including the cutting of pay, for councillors found guilty, and stronger protections for council employees who report bad behaviour.

Advertisement

Finally, it called for “mechanisms to enable councils to recover or offset significant costs incurred in responding to complaints that are found to be without merit or constitute an abuse of the complaints process”. The inquiry will hold four public hearings this month and report back to state parliament in November.
