The Suns refused to consider trading him last year, and Humphrey has not made a trade request this year. The Hawks are readying to bring in Gold Coast’s restricted free agent spearhead Ben King – with the Suns highly likely to accept a compensation pick rather than force a trade – and still want to trade for former Essendon captain Zach Merrett. The Blues acquired Ben Ainsworth from Gold Coast last year, plus ex-Swans Will Hayward and Ollie Florent, but are likely to remain aggressive with Chris Davies and Graham Wright overseeing list management. Decision time looms Carlton’s must-win clash against the Western Bulldogs on Sunday will be something of an audition for Bulldogs defender Buku Khamis as he weighs up his future at the club.

The Bulldogs upped their offer to the free agent to four years to match, in tenure, the offer from Carlton as they attempt to retain the popular Khamis. Versatile Bulldogs defender Buku Khamis. Getty Images The 26-year-old will spend the next fortnight, at least, deciding his future after examining offers from both clubs, with the Bulldogs increasingly hopeful he will remain at “the Kennel”. Khamis wanted to join the Blues at the end of last season as he felt starved of opportunity, but this season has proven the key role he can play at the Dogs. He has played every match, but is aware he is best suited as a third tall defender who intercepts in the air rather, than as a key defender expected to lock down opponents.

Cody Walker watch The one downside to Carlton’s on-field resurgence under interim coach Josh Fraser is that the equation to match a draft bid on prized father-son midfielder Cody Walker becomes that much harder. The Blues would score a 10 per cent discount on the teenage star if they finish between 11th and 18th, which is still a possibility with two rounds to go. Getty Images Walker is widely tipped to attract a bid at pick No.2 in this year’s draft, and Carlton can use only two picks to match – another new rule. That Swans pick would slide from No.17 to No.18 in the aforementioned King scenario, so Carlton’s combined draft value index points would be 2112. The No.2 pick is worth 2481 points.

The Blues can go into deficit in a future draft by a maximum of 412 points (this would result in them picking later in 2027), meaning a glorious September run could come at great cost. NationalQueenslandQueensland councils ‘Avoiding accountability’: Council takes aim at mayor on medical leave Julius Dennis August 12, 2026 — 12:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A south-east Queensland council appears to have taken a dig at its own mayor in a submission to a parliamentary inquiry, recommending any councillor on extended leave should be subject to a misconduct investigation. Redland City Council mayor Jos Mitchell has been on medical leave since May. The council recently said she would not return until at least the end of October, with deputy mayor Julie Talty in her chair. Jos Mitchell has been on leave since May. Dan Peled The council of Redlands, south-east of Brisbane, has been a hotbed of discontent for years, leading the state in conduct complaints received by the Office of the Independent Assessor in the 2024-25 financial year and the first half of 2025-26.

Advertisement

Of the 1008 complaints received in 2024-25, 114 were about Redlands councillors. Mitchell was the subject of about 50 in the 18 months after she elected as mayor, and she alleged they were used as a political tool against her. The former Labor state government reformed the OIA to streamline its processes in 2023, and the current LNP government made further changes to narrow its scope in March this year, before announcing a parliamentary inquiry into the councillor conduct framework in June. Redlands led the state in OIA complaints last year. Matt Dennien The inquiry, run by the Local Government, Small Business and Customer Service Committee, is considering the effectiveness of the current system – based around the OIA and the Councillor Conduct Tribunal – and potential changes to the Local Government Act. It received 40 submissions before they closed this week, with the Redlands submission including a pointed recommendation apparently directed at its own mayor.

Advertisement

“The definition of ‘misconduct’, which will continue to be a discipline matter, needs to be broadened to include the more serious councillor conduct breaches and to address non-performance, not just bad behaviour,” it said. “As we have seen, a councillor can effectively avoid accountability by simply being absent. A councillor on extended leave should then be subject to a misconduct investigation.” Related Article Queensland councils ‘Loopholes’ in council complaints system can be weaponised: mayor Mitchell’s leave has been the subject of heated online debate since May, with other councillors and former local federal MP and mayoral candidate Andrew Laming often weighing in. The mayor has been largely silent, but posted on Facebook this month claiming there was “a fair bit of fake news” about her absence.

Advertisement

“I’ve been dealing with a number of health issues, one requiring major surgery and recuperation, over the last 12 weeks,” she wrote. “I have of course provided medical certificates and I am focused on recovery … I look forward to returning as soon as possible.” That post followed a now-deleted Facebook post, written by her family members, taking aim at local government department boss Bronwyn Blagoev for what they deemed politically opportunistic comments following the departure of a department-appointed governance adviser at the council. “The mayor’s prolonged absence meant that key opportunities to address critical governance challenges and foster stronger leadership were missed,” Blagoev had said. The Redlands submission also called for a properly resourced external body to investigate councillor conduct outside the OIA, stronger penalties, including the cutting of pay, for councillors found guilty, and stronger protections for council employees who report bad behaviour.

Advertisement

Finally, it called for “mechanisms to enable councils to recover or offset significant costs incurred in responding to complaints that are found to be without merit or constitute an abuse of the complaints process”. The inquiry will hold four public hearings this month and report back to state parliament in November. title: Gold is glittering again – but that’s not necessarily good news
text:
Advertisement

BusinessMarketsGold Opinion Gold is glittering again – but that’s not necessarily good news Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist August 12, 2026 — 11:58am

August 12, 2026 — 11:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After a near-six-month hiatus, the gold price has suddenly surged again. That’s probably not an encouraging sign of things to come. The price peaked, at record levels, above $US5300 ($7500) an ounce just ahead of the start of the war in the Middle East at the end of February. It then steadily reversed course, falling below $US4000 an ounce last month, before surging again to trade above $4400 an ounce this week. In just over a week it has climbed more than 8 per cent. There were obvious catalysts for the movements in both directions. America and Israel’s war with Iran have been weighing on the gold price - until now. Bloomberg The United States and Israel’s attack on Iran, which sent oil prices soaring and raised expectations of inflation, punctured gold’s record run.

Advertisement

The US Federal Reserve Board’s decision to leave its policy rate unchanged at last month’s meeting, and the inability of its new chair Kevin Warsh to dispel concerns that he will do Donald Trump’s bidding, has been a significant influence over the metal’s recent resurgence. Last year’s gold rush was ignited by a speech given by Warsh’s predecessor, Jerome Powell, at the annual economic talkfest at Jackson Hole in Wyoming, where he signalled the start of an interest rate easing cycle that the Fed followed up with three rate cuts. If investors fear that America’s finances might corrupt its monetary policies, the gold market looks like the obvious – perhaps the only – place to shelter. The Fed seemed to be shifting its focus from inflation to protecting growth. Gold’s key appeal is that it provides a hedge against inflation, so that apparent shift in priorities set its market alight. There’s an inverse relationship between the gold price and interest rates. Lower rates – because gold generates no income but has holding and opportunity costs – are positive for the price.

Advertisement

The price has been aided by last week’s weak US jobs data, which blunted the market’s expectations of a September rate rise, although inflation data this week could complicate assessments of the state of the world’s largest economy. Related Article Opinion

Federal Reserve Meddler-in-chief: Trump is up to his old tricks again Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Weakening economic growth and sustained high, or rising, levels of inflation – stagflation – are, however, positive for gold, so even if the inflation rate remains elevated, it’s not necessarily threatening to the price. In those circumstances, gold’s “safe haven” status and its inverse correlation with inflation tend to support the price. The Fed’s rate actions last year sparked discussion about the “debasement trade” and “fiscal dominance”, or the fear that government debt and debt-servicing costs were so out of control that central banks have to inflate their way out of the fiscal noose. For investors, that means a dash for safe assets, gold in particular. The US has a debt issue, with gross federal government debt soon to hit $US40 trillion, or 124 per cent of GDP.

Advertisement

In the second Trump administration, nearly $US4 trillion will have been added in just over 18 months, with the country’s debt-to-GDP ratio blowing out from 5.8 per cent to about 6.5 per cent of GDP this financial year, according to the Congressional Budget Office’s latest projections. The government’s net interest bill is nearing $US1 trillion, which is bigger than the Defence Department’s budget (or has been, before the “War Department” asked for $US1.5 trillion of funding next financial year). The US isn’t alone with its debt mountain. In the post-COVID era, most Western governments have balance sheets that are stretched to unsustainable levels. But it is the epicentre of the world’s financial system and its Treasury securities are the alternative safe haven to gold for investors. If investors fear that America’s finances might corrupt its monetary policies, the gold market looks like the obvious – perhaps the only – place to shelter.

Advertisement

The gold price over the past year has clearly been driven by a number of different factors, even if US inflation and interest rates might provide the most significant macro backdrop. Trump’s trade wars, which also affect inflation and generate geopolitical instability, and his actual war in the Middle East, with its impact on oil prices (and subsequently inflation), have also driven ebbs and flows in the gold price as their fortunes have fluctuated. Trump’s tariffs have been a moving feast as he’s imposed, withdrawn and threatened duties, and then been forced to change their legal basis entirely after they’ve been ruled illegal in the courts. Similarly, the war in the Middle East has been on the verge of ending dozens of times, according to Trump, but the conflict continues. That’s caused some volatility in the gold price, but the impacts have been quite clear.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war Trump’s great humiliation: Middle East may be entering a post-American era Peter Hartcher Political and international editor When investors thought the Fed was likely to raise US rates to head off higher tariff and oil-driven increases in inflation, the gold price trended down. Very recently, when it looked like there might be a deal to end the war and the likelihood of the Fed raising rates receded, they sparked up again. While this year has produced a volatile run for the gold price, there’s an underlying, longer-term trend towards high prices. That started in 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine and the G7 economies froze Russia’s foreign exchange reserves held offshore, weaponising the US dollar’s dominance of the financial system. Since that moment, central banks have doubled their purchases of gold, which has now overtaken US Treasury securities as their biggest reserve asset.

Advertisement

Advertisement

If the “carry trades” (using cheap Japanese funding to buy higher-yielding assets elsewhere) that have flourished over nearly 30 years were to suddenly unwind, and/or Japanese investors and Japan’s government were to repatriate the trillions of dollars in US treasuries, equities and other assets they hold, it would ignite another global financial crisis, with the US again at its centre. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war Trump’s video game war has the world in an economic spiral There’s also mounting concern about the valuations, the rapidly increasing reliance on increasingly complex debt structures and the absence of cash flows that characterise the artificial intelligence boom and the infrastructure being built for it. AI has become central to the US market and economy. The leverage associated with it has grown rapidly and is very substantial. Yet the rate of investment in AI outstrips the cash being generated from it. It’s an implosion waiting to happen, unless the AI companies can dramatically boost their cash generation.

Advertisement

That’s a tricky backdrop for Warsh when he makes his first appearance at Jackson Hole late this month. If he fails to convince markets that he is committed to driving the US inflation rate down, the smiles on the faces of gold bugs might get even broader. Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn says first home buyers are likely to start coming into the property market in greater numbers once they expect interest rates to fall, after it reported a 15 per cent drop in mortgage lending since the budget. Even so, Comyn also said applications had stabilised this month, and the bank still expected growth in housing credit over the year ahead.

The government says its clampdown on property investor tax breaks is aimed at helping first home buyers afford a home, and Comyn said he expected a pickup in demand once there was “anticipation of rate cuts.” When asked if the government’s changes had helped first home buyers, Comyn said house prices had peaked in March, and “fallen in the four months since then, I think about 2.5 per cent.“ “Now, obviously, there’s a range of different, forecasts, but you would imagine that, when rates look like they might change, we’ll see an increase,” Comyn said. The Reserve Bank has raised the cash rate three times this year, taking it to 4.35 per cent, and economists are split over whether interest rates have now peaked. CBA economists believe the RBA will keep rates unchanged for the rest of this year, and are forecasting two rate cuts next year. Comyn’s remarks on housing came after the bank notched up $11 billion in cash profit fuelled by growth across its vast loan and deposit portfolios, as it also warned economic growth was slowing amid higher interest rates and inflation.

Cash net profit after tax rose 7 per cent in the year to June, as its operating income grew by 6 per cent, helped by growth in CBA’s key markets of home loans, business loans, consumer lending and household and business deposits. CBA on Wednesday said cash net profit after tax rose 7 per cent in the year to June. Oscar Colman Despite strong growth in the year to June, however, CBA also said new applications for mortgages had fallen 15 per cent since the May budget, as the housing market slows due to higher interest rates and a tightening in tax concessions for property investors. The bank also said costs from soured loans had increased due to cost of living pressures and increased economic uncertainty. Chief executive Matt Comyn said the economy had been resilient, helped by low unemployment and solid investment, though economic growth was feeling the effects of higher interest rates and inflation. “Growth is slowing, with higher interest rates and inflation placing

uneven pressure on household incomes and economic activity,” he said.

Home loans How to benefit from the coming mortgage price war Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor “Housing activity has softened from a high base.” The results also provided more evidence that mortgage applications have slowed sharply across the banking industry since the May budget, which included moves to clamp down on borrowing by property investors. CBA said its home loan applications had fallen 15 per cent since the May budget – though this trend appeared to have stabilised recently. The 15 per cent drop compares with Westpac this week saying its home loan applications were down 20 per cent since the budget, while late last month National Australia Bank said its Australian home loan applications were down 15 per cent in the June quarter compared with the March quarter.

“Housing activity has softened from a high base. Application volumes appear to have stabilised in recent weeks. Businesses continue to manage higher input costs and supply uncertainty,” Comyn said. Analysts had expected full-year cash profits of about $10.85 billion. CBA raised its final dividend to $2.70, up from $2.60 last year. CBA’s numbers are seen as a bellwether for the Australian economy, and the banking giant’s results showed its expenses for impaired loans had increased by 47 per cent in the June half compared with the March half, to $788 million. The bank’s net interest margin, which compares bank funding costs with the price of loans, edged 2 basis points higher over the year to 2.05 per cent. CBA, Australia’s largest bank, said that during the year to June it had grown in line with or faster than the industry average in its five core markets: home loans, business loans, consumer finance products such as credit cards, household deposits and business deposits. “It is the first time CBA has achieved this and the first time any major Australian bank has done so in the past 15 years,” CBA said. title: ‘Frustrating’: NSW Health minister seeks urgent update from TGA over defibrillators

The NSW government has demanded an explanation from the health watchdog over its suspension on the sale of defibrillators used in the state’s ambulances. The Therapeutic Goods Administration suspended the registration of the corpuls defibrillator late last month, meaning it will banned from sale, but has refused to say why. NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said he will ask the TGA for clarification. Louise Kennerley “I’ll be writing to the TGA to see if they could give us a little bit more information,” Park told a press conference on Wednesday morning. “They’ve made a decision not to disclose the details … that can be a little bit frustrating.” The government and NSW Ambulance continue to assert that the devices are safe for patient use, despite widespread complaints from paramedics, including reports of the device failing to discharge a shock.

Advertisement

It comes after this masthead revealed on Tuesday that a senior NSW Ambulance figure told staff that the corplus 3 and corplus 3T defibrillators recorded 1229 failures in 2025 alone. Related Article Exclusive

Ambulance ‘I am not happy’: Top paramedic dumps on disappointing defibrillator Park said that “not all of those have been serious failures. It could be a lead not working. It could be a range of different areas”. He said the TGA had not instructed his government to remove the devices from circulation, but that an incident management team had been established. “I’m still confident, based on the advice of the NSW Ambulance ... as well as the TGA, that this should remain in our ambulances and form a part of the life-saving equipment that we have for people,” he said.

Advertisement

NSW opposition health spokesperson Sarah Mitchell said it was “pretty concerning that the health minister hasn’t been made aware already by the TGA what the major concerns are”. This masthead revealed on Tuesday that Marty Nichols, Ambulance NSW’s associate director of clinical practice, sympathised with paramedics who had raised concerns about the devices on an internal forum of more than 4000 members, where he said they had a “right to be disappointed”. The corpuls3T modular defibrillator. title: David Chandler wants to build housing that people can afford. And says he’s the man to do it
text:
Advertisement

Exclusive PoliticsNSWCity life David Chandler wants to build housing that people can afford. And says he’s the man to do it Max Maddison August 12, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former NSW building commissioner David Chandler says he would be willing to return to public life to address “absolute market failure” in the missing middle apartment sector, laying down his solution to address the state’s housing crisis by building thousands of cheaper dwellings for those who have been priced out. Two years after resigning as the inaugural building commissioner, Chandler said he would apply to head the delivery of his “intentionally disruptive” project – named MM3 – if the Minns government adopted it, saying the housing initiative required someone with a reputation for “getting stuff done”. Former NSW building commissioner David Chandler has declared he would return to government to help solve the state’s housing crisis. Sam Mooy Chandler’s intervention comes with the Minns government struggling to materially lift the delivery of housing supply despite introducing a raft of planning reforms. “The crisis is so severe that you can’t park this under a bushel any longer. It’s time for some challenging ideas to surface,” Chandler said.

Advertisement

“The first thing is acknowledging that the system is not delivering for the people who most need it.” The project’s intent is to deliver lower-cost apartments which have become unfeasible under current market conditions. The delivery of units at a more affordable price point would help people on the cusp of owning a home, using small and medium-sized builders who were looking to level up from greenfield sites to apartment projects, envisaged to range from six to 24 dwellings. It outlines an avenue for delivering newly built apartments priced at less than $1 million. Chandler said his model could reduce building costs by at least 20 per cent, noting developers normally needed to attract a $1.2 million sale price and generate profit margins of around 20 per cent. Nguluway DesignInc’s three- to four-storey apartment building design for the NSW government mid-rise pattern book could be one of the projects built under Chandler’s model. NSW government By using government-approved pattern book designs, Chandler said construction costs would be reduced as builders repeated the same project “50 or 60 times”, creating efficiencies and economies of scale as identical materials could be purchased for a year’s worth of projects.

Advertisement

With the government acquiring the land needed for these projects, apartments wouldn’t need to return the profit margin developers required. Related Article City life ‘Waiting for a miracle’: How the cost of building a Sydney house skyrocketed to $1m The MM3 model would deliver a typical 85 square metre, two-bedroom apartment at a cost of around $350,000 to $400,000 for construction, with land costs “exceeding no more than $500,000” per dwelling. It would also mitigate the risk of buyers bearing the risk of builders failing before the projects were finished, as government would provide a completion guarantee. Chandler, who has 50 years’ experience in construction, said apartments remained unaffordable for those trying to enter the market, despite all the concessions government had given developers, such as greater floor-space ratios.

Advertisement

“We’ve certainly reached a point where, for a certain part of the market, there is absolute market failure,” he said. Related Article City life ‘I don’t earn enough to rent anything’: How Sydney’s grand housing vision was whittled away Entry-level housing should be determined by what the purchaser can afford to pay, Chandler said, rather than what real estate agents dictate is easier to sell. “We’ve lost our way where developers have always gone to a real estate agent or a marketing agency to say, ‘How will we get this project off the ground?’, ‘Well, it’s got to be bigger. It’s got to have marble bench tops’,” he said. The strategy targets delivery of 4000 new units by the third year of operation. A program office, within an existing government department, would facilitate the delivery of the program. The proposal is designed to have a five to seven-year shelf life, providing a model for the private sector to replicate and ultimately take over from government.

Advertisement

“No one has sat down and thought through the fact that there’s a very seriously disenfranchised group of prospective people who want to become self-sufficient in housing to actually get on that ladder, and all the current mechanisms are synthetic at best,” Chandler said. Chandler, who is due to give evidence at the ICAC’s Operation Rosny public hearing, declined to say what he would reveal. The ICAC has heard that Liberal operatives plotted to have Chandler dismissed as building commissioner. Chandler is not a target of the inquiry. Asked about his willingness to return to public life, Chandler said if the government adopted his housing proposal, he would apply with others to run the MM3 program office, declaring the project needed an “unambiguous mandate” similar to when he was brought in to clean up the state’s building sector in 2019. “There are very few bureaucrats who have got the ability or the guts to actually come up with something that will be disruptive,” he said. “I have a reputation for getting stuff done, so there’s no value in giving a challenge like this to somebody who doesn’t have a reputation for getting stuff done. So I put my hand up, and I’d be quite happy to compete with somebody else who’s got a similar sort of capacity.”

title: A beer emoji and a mystery injury: Dolphins boss addresses Cooper drinking incident
text:
Advertisement

Analysis SportSwimmingSwimming A beer emoji and a mystery injury: Dolphins boss addresses Cooper drinking incident Tom Decent August 12, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Irvine: Several days after skipping the final night of swimming at the Commonwealth Games to go out drinking instead of supporting his Australian teammates and attending a mandatory team meeting, Isaac Cooper posted a photo to Instagram with a beer emoji in the caption that raised eyebrows. “Cheers Glasgow 🍻,” Cooper wrote to his 41,000 Instagram followers. “It was real. Onto the next.” Isaac Cooper competes at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Getty Images Within hours, Cooper – who this masthead can reveal split with his coach, Olympian Ash Delaney, on the eve of the Commonwealth Games – had deleted the beer emoji. Cooper changed the caption from “Cheers Glasgow” to “Peace out Glasgow”.

Advertisement

Isaac Cooper’s since deleted caption on Instagram. Instagram One user noted in the comments that it was a “wild caption”. Cooper liked that comment. For an athlete who, only a few weeks earlier, had told this masthead how proud he was to have been appointed to the Dolphins’ leadership group, Cooper’s post spoke volumes. Australia head coach Rohan Taylor, who declined to be interviewed in the days after this masthead revealed the incident in Glasgow, was asked at a Pan Pacific Championships press conference in Irvine, California, on Tuesday whether he was surprised by Cooper’s social media post featuring a beer emoji. Taylor offered no opinion. “I don’t have social media, so I didn’t see it,” he said. “I heard about it but I didn’t see it.”

Advertisement

On the day Cooper went missing in Glasgow, having been spotted drinking at the bar at Australian team headquarters, Taylor was furious the 22-year-old backstroker was not at the pool supporting his teammates. In the days that followed, satirical website The Betoota Advocate published a story under the headline: “God Forbid A Queenslander Goes To A Pub While On Tour”. Cooper decided to reshare the post on Instagram, not that Taylor would have known. A satirical Betoota Advocate article which Isaac Cooper shared on Instagram. Instagram Swimming great and fellow Queenslander Kaylee McKeown, who did not compete at the Commonwealth Games, liked the Advocate’s post. In the comments section, Louisa Forrester, the mother of Australian swimmer Jenna Forrester, wrote: “What a dumb and ignorant article”.

Advertisement

Pinning down a timeline of the Cooper incident in Scotland has been difficult, with Swimming Australia not forthcoming with information relating to Cooper’s mishap. Taylor could have sent Cooper home to make a statement about the standards expected within the team. He chose not to. Isaac Cooper poses for a photo before the Commonwealth Games. Delly Carr Taylor could have also been proactive and taken away Cooper’s leadership role. Instead, that was Cooper’s own doing, according to Swimming Australia. Meanwhile, no details have been given about Cooper’s explanation when he sat down with team officials to account for his failure to not show up at the pool.

Advertisement

This is an athlete who, four years ago, was sent home by Taylor from a training camp ahead of the Commonwealth Games in Birmingham for the misuse of prescription medication, including giving sleeping pills to teammates. Cooper said last month he believed he was harshly treated then. Swimming Australia’s statement on August 3, released in the hours after the closing ceremony, read: “Isaac did not attend the final night of the swimming competition or final team meeting in Glasgow which is in conflict with team expectations. Isaac has since voluntarily stood down from the team’s athlete leadership group. Swimming Australia will not be making any further comment.” Dolphins head coach Rohan Taylor. Getty Images Taylor was equally coy on the eve of Pan Pacs, which begin on Wednesday (Thursday AEST). He was asked to provide a timeline and, in particular, why Cooper had decided to pull out of his 100m backstroke final – an event held on the final night of competition when he was out drinking. “The night before [July 28], both he and [breaststroker] Sienna Toohey wanted to pull out of their [individual] events the next day to save themselves for the relay,” Taylor said. “Sienna had to do the heats in the morning and Isaac was doing the heat. So they pulled out for that purpose.”

Advertisement

However, that explanation contradicts a post on Cooper’s official Facebook page, which claimed he did not race the 100m backstroke final because of a back injury. It is unclear who has been posting to the page on Cooper’s behalf, but it links to his official website and lists contact details for his management team, who were approached for comment. “Isaac has made the difficult decision to withdraw from tomorrow’s 100m backstroke final at the Commonwealth Games,” the post read. A post on Isaac Cooper’s officials Instagram page during the Commonwealth Games. Facebook “Following further assessment by the Australian team doctor, Isaac has been diagnosed with a spine fracture. While this is not drastic it will require some treatment before Pan Pacs, so Isaac chose to swim in the men’s 4x100m medley relay heats tonight.”

Advertisement

Asked about the back injury and whether he was aware of it, Taylor did not confirm its existence. “All I know is he’d come to me and spoke to me about saving himself for the medley relay,” Taylor said. Isaac Cooper failed to attend the final night in the pool and a team meeting the same evening. Getty So, was Cooper really nursing a spine fracture significant enough to withdraw from an individual Commonwealth Games final? He was eighth fastest into the 100m backstroke final and long odds to win it. There are also differences between Cooper and Toohey’s situations. Cooper had qualified for the 100m backstroke final on the penultimate night of racing, whereas Toohey still needed to swim a 200m breaststroke heat on the morning of the final day as well as fulfil her duties in the women’s 4x100m medley relay.

Advertisement

Meanwhile, the notion of Cooper “saving” himself for a 4x100m medley relay heat is perplexing given Australia’s heat time of 3:34.67 – Cooper was the lead-off swimmer – was almost 10 seconds faster than eighth-fastest qualifier Namibia. Australia was not going to miss the final. With backstroker Henry Allan then selected to swim the men’s medley relay final later that evening, Cooper could have still contested the 100m backstroke final but was nowhere to be seen. Taylor was also asked for clarity on Swimming Australia’s statement that Cooper had voluntarily stood down from the leadership group. “The conversations I’ve had with Isaac are between Isaac and I,” Taylor said. “At the end of the day, we’re here and excited to be in Irvine and focused on Pan Pacs and building on that. He’s here to race.” Was Taylor disappointed Cooper had been out drinking?

Advertisement

“We want our team to be united and together,” Taylor said. “And so anytime [something] like that happens, it’s always something we have to address. We did and we moved on.” Isaac Cooper (centre) ahead of Pan Pacs in Irvine. Swimming Australia On the subject of Cooper no longer being coached by Delaney, Taylor said: “That was something that happened after trials. They worked together until he left to come [overseas]. I’ve been talking to him [Cooper] and working on where he might end up and where he wants to train after this. That’s something we’ll work on once we get home.” Splitting with a coach on the eve of a major event is unusual. Delaney did not travel to Glasgow or Irvine because he was not selected by Swimming Australia as part of the Dolphins’ coaching staff.

Advertisement

Brazilian Olympic bronze medallist Bruno Fratus also weighed in on X. Related Article Swimming The Pan Pacs are the entree before LA Olympics. Here are the five races not to miss “Isaac is so talented and [has] a very bright future in front of him if he gets his head in the right place. And it [is] absolutely unacceptable to behave like this while on a team,” Fratus wrote. “But that being said ... do athletes even get paid to perform such leadership roles?” Cooper is yet to publicly explain what happened in Glasgow. Requests through Swimming Australia’s media department to interview him over the past week have been unsuccessful. He races on Wednesday (Thursday AEST) in the men’s 50m butterfly. For now, all there is to go on are his interactions on social media.

Advertisement

“I’m loving being in the US and taking in every minute,” Cooper wrote on Instagram. “Keen to race again.” “I made it [to Irvine] … who’d have thunk.” One of Cooper’s followers commented on his latest post: “This calls for a celebratory beer”. Cooper responded: “I agree”. For the Dolphins’ sake, hopefully those beers can wait until after Irvine.

title: Musician killed in ski resort tragedy named
text:
The victim of a ski resort tragedy this week has been named as a rising music star with more than 1.1 million YouTube views to his name.

Talae Rodden, who performed under the name RiceWine, died on Monday on Mt Buller Rd in northeastern Victoria when a tree suddenly fell on his car.

The 27-year-old was a passenger in the car with his mother Sally.

Talae Rodden died after a tree fell on his car. Picture: GoFundMe

His mother suffered serious injuries and was rushed to hospital, but Mr Rodden died at the scene.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Now, his local ski club is rallying around his family as they come to terms with the loss of the talented musician.

University Ski Club has set up a GoFundMe page to support the family in their hour of need. It has already raised a staggering $113,000.

"The Rodden family are much-loved members of the Mount Buller, Merrijig and Mansfield communities," the post reads.

He performed under the name RiceWine.

"There are simply no words to describe the shock and heartbreak felt by everyone who knows this beautiful family.

"Talae was a talented and much-loved young man, cherished by his family, friends and so many people who had the privilege of knowing him.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"His loss has left an enormous hole in the communities he was so much a part of."

More than 750 people so far have contributed to the fundraiser, which will go towards the costs of his funeral and medical expenses to support his mother through her recovery from the disaster.

Mr Rodden with family members. Picture: GoFundMe

Mr Rodden was working to build a career for himself as a singer-songwriter.

Under the name RiceWine, he performed at several high-profile events, including SXSW in Sydney and Fest by Inner West in October 2025.

His most popular song, Summer Spent, has been listened to more than 1.1 million times on YouTube since he released it four years ago.

He leaves behind mother Sally, father Cha and his brother Jared.
